title: Inference Contract Narrative
body:
One‑pager concept: 'The Inference Contract' — a simple, pragmatic framing to explain why teams should treat inference as a service-level contract rather than a collection of knobs.

Goal: give sales, product marketing, and engineering a crisp, consumer-facing narrative that ties Redwood’s capabilities to the single promise that matters to product teams: predictable user experiences at a known cost.

Why this framing?
- Many buyers talk about models or hardware. Customers actually care about experience delivered to end users: latency, availability, cost per active user.
- 'Contract' language reframes choices as obligations (SLA, fallbacks, predictable degradation) instead of features to be tuned.
- This helps us sell reserved/dedicated capacity, private deployments, and the observability stack as parts of the same commitment.

Core thesis (one line):
Redwood is the inference partner that signs the contract to make LLM features behave like any other production service — reliably, affordably, and auditable.

Mission statement (short):
Enable engineering teams to ship LLM-powered experiences with the economics and reliability they expect from modern cloud services.

Key pillars (customer-facing):
1) Predictable latency and graceful degradation
   - SLO-driven routing, automatic fallbacks to compatible model variants, per-route latency guarantees for paid tiers.
   - Message for builders: "No surprise p99 spikes in peak traffic."
2) Transparent unit economics
   - Per-token + per-embedding meter with token-level cost breakdown in Console; recommendations to trade cost for latency or quality.
   - Message: "Know your $/active user before you scale."
3) Operational ownership, not just a blackbox
   - Rollouts, canaries, tracing hooks, prompt-level evals, and audit logs to tie regressions to releases.
   - Message: "You retain control — we provide the guardrails."
4) Deployment parity across modes
   - Same API and operational model across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private so you can move without re-architecting.
   - Message: "Ship on hosted, scale to private — no vendor lock-in for your stack."

Distinctive proof points (quick bullets for sales):
- Kin tests: internal benchmark where we kept p99 latency within SLA during synthetic 3x peak bursts using fallback routing and KV caching. (link to perf deck in linked_artifacts)
- Cost-savings playbook: customers reduced per-call CPU/GPU time by 27% with batching + quantization suggestions from Redwood Optimize.
- Security/compliance: Private control plane + KMS integrations used in two regulated pilots (healthcare and fintech).

Competitor positioning (brief):
- Generic cloud endpoints: trade predictable SLOs and model ops for convenience — we emphasize inference-level SLAs and rollout primitives.
- Model-access APIs: good model access but not the economics/observability — we sell a contract (SLA + cost transparency) not just tokens.
- Self-hosted inference runtimes: flexible but heavy lift — we provide ops primitives and migration paths (Dedicated/Private) to reduce build costs.

Tactical messaging (short lines for site and deck):
- Headline: 'Inference that behaves like a service.'
- Subhead: 'Predictable latency. Transparent cost. Operational control.'
- 2‑sentence pitch: 'Redwood helps engineering teams deliver LLM features that meet the same reliability and cost expectations as the rest of their stack. We combine a high‑throughput runtime with rollouts, tracing, and cost insights so you can treat inference as a contract — not a gamble.'

Buyer personas and hooks: 
- Startup product lead (PLG): stress quick time to value + clear upgrade path to dedicated capacity when cost predictability is needed.
- Platform/infra lead: emphasize API parity, rollout primitives, observability, and SSO/KMS controls.
- Security/compliance buyer: highlight private mode, audit logs, and integration options.

Open questions / trade-offs to discuss (internal):
- How explicit do we make SLAs in public pricing vs enterprise contracts? (sales/legal input needed)
- Do we publish sample p99/p50 numbers for common models and sequence lengths or keep them in gated benchmarks?
- Messaging risk: "contract" language may read as legalistic — test softer variants ("service pledge", "behavior guarantee").

Launch checklist (short):
- Lock final headline and 2-sentence pitch (product + marketing)
- Create 1‑pager datasheet (for sales + website) with three examples (chat, summarization, embeddings) and measured p99 numbers
- Add gated benchmark page for technical buyers (link to perf deck)
- Sales enablement: 30‑minute training + objection handling doc (SLAs, cost tradeoffs, migration stories)

Notes to self / rough drafts: 
- Possible tagline: 'Build features. Sign the contract.' (too blunt?)
- Demo idea: live compare of same request across hosted vs fallback routing under load — show degradation instead of outage.
- Use customer quote template: 'We moved to Redwood because our chat feature stopped failing during peaks — and the bill became predictable.'

Next steps:
- Align with Product on what SLA language we can promise in public vs. private docs (owner: Marco)
- Draft datasheet + perf appendix (owner: Jenna)
- Wind up a short A/B test for two taglines on landing page (owner: Asha)

References / useful links: Confluence (INFERENCE-PROPS-874), Jira (GTM-3421), internal perf deck (github:pr/6213).

End of doc.
